Pictures

Two held notes are the two channels, so the interval under your hands is the figure on the screen: a fifth draws 2:3 and stands still, a third walks. Dyad reads the two most recent notes and puts the lower on X; mono takes the newest note as the pitch and leaves the interval to the menu. A note is also the one pitch on this page that is not estimated, which is why the lag, the tuner and the timebase can be told to take it as read. The port and the learned controllers are under Settings → MIDI.

Arpeggiator

Plays a held chord a note at a time at the tempo. Letting go stops it; its notes go out through MIDI out.

Bar

A keyboard or a sequencer sending MIDI clock sets the tempo while it runs, and its Start restarts the locked oscillators; From says which. Bar is where the page is in the music, counted in fours: the score reads its columns from it, so its first column is always a downbeat. Stop holds it and silences the score; Start puts it back to the one and restarts the locked oscillators with it. A tap is the one while it runs. A device's Start, Stop and Continue do the same, on its first tick, and under its clock the bar counts its ticks. The arpeggiator follows your hands, not the bar.

Audio
What is it

A microphone is never sent to the speakers: what comes out of them goes back into it, and that is a feedback loop. A line input has no ear — a keyboard does not hear the room — so it may be monitored, and that is a claim you are making about what is plugged in rather than something the browser can tell. Get it wrong with a microphone selected and the loop is real, so wear headphones the first time.

What you hear that way has been round the converter twice and through the page's own buffers: the figure given is the browser's own, which is the output side only and a floor rather than the whole trip. Tens of milliseconds is normal and a keyboard player will feel it. The setup that does not suffer it is hearing the instrument directly and letting this page only look. A band split is not monitored at all.

MIDI

Setting up a Nord Electro: it connects twice. USB carries MIDI only, and the left and right line outs go to a stereo line input — that is the organ itself, and the rotary, chorus and vibrato are genuinely stereo, so X–Y draws a moving figure rather than the diagonal a mono microphone gives. On the keyboard, System Menu 12 → Send & Receive, or no panel control transmits at all; Local on to hear the organ while the generator draws under your hands, off to play the generator alone. Move a drawbar, a pedal or the swell and it learns as a source you can put on any control — CC 11 is the swell pedal and exists only if one is plugged into the control pedal jack.

Web MIDI needs a secure page, and inside an iframe it needs the embedding page to grant it. The published artifact is such an iframe and does not, so the keyboard works on the GitHub Pages copy and not there. Safari has no Web MIDI at all.

Layer B has its own shape, level and envelope, and its own drawbars and morph, and nothing else: its pitches are the keys it is given, and the kind and the modulation are the generator's. Edit A in the keyboard section puts the panel back.

Tuning

A Lissajous figure closes when the two frequencies are a ratio of small whole numbers — which is what a consonant interval is. In just tuning a fifth is exactly 2:3 and stands still; in equal it is slightly off, and the figure turns at the rate the interval beats. At a unison the phase decides it: 0° a diagonal, 90° a circle.

The beam draws one unbroken line, so edges it cannot reach without lifting are retraced rather than jumped — a doubled line is the same pixels, a jump would be a permanent chord across the middle. The envelope only does anything while the keyboard is driving the generator — with nothing plugged in the amplitude is the slider and nothing else, exactly as it was. A second note while one is still held changes the pitch without starting the envelope again, which is what makes a run of notes a phrase rather than a row of attacks; glide slides between them instead of stepping. The envelope is also a source: send Envelope to the rotation or the ratio and the figure opens as the note does.

Key and tempo
off
120 BPM

One key and one tempo for the page. Quantise takes the generator's pitch, after everything patched onto it, to the nearest note of the key: put a slow oscillator or the photocell on the frequency and it plays a melody in the key instead of a siren. A key you play that is outside the scale is moved too, which is what a quantiser does. It waits a tenth of a semitone past half-way before it steps, and never steps faster than forty times a second, so a pitch resting between two notes does not flicker. Glide slides between the steps. Chromatic, the default, quantises to the nearest semitone. The harmonograph and the figures are not quantised: a pendulum's two hertz is not a note.

An oscillator's Sync, on the Sources tab, locks its rate to the tempo in note values. Tap sets the tempo from your taps and starts the locked oscillators on the last one. Where the tempo comes from and where the bar is are in the Clock section, behind Advanced.

Saved setups live in this browser and nowhere else. A setup code is the whole configuration as text — copy it, send it, paste it back.

AC blocks what is not moving, so a converter with a DC offset does not push the trace off the screen. It is a one-pole high pass, and its corner is where it starts to take things away: low and it only removes a slow drift, high and it thins the bottom of the signal as well. Ten hertz is where a bench scope's AC coupling usually sits. The same corner reaches the speakers when they are on the shaped side, from one set of numbers — the screen and the speakers cannot disagree about what AC coupling is.

Full scale is the level that reaches the top of the graticule — drop it to open up a quiet signal.

Display
0°
Numbers read

Turns the figure on the screen. Worth little by hand and a great deal pointed at something: send Level to it and the picture turns as you play, which is the difference between a shape that sits there and one that answers.

On a stereo pair it turns the signal: the lanes are rotated before the trigger sees them, so Y–T, the figure and — on the shaped side — the speakers are all the same rotation. On a band split or the lag lane it only turns the figure, because those are not a stereo image and mixing the bass band into the treble is not what the knob says it does.

Numbers read is what the cells along the bottom, the tuner and the correlation bar are about. Signal is what arrived and is the default, so turning the picture leaves every reading exactly where it was — the same arithmetic on the same samples, not a close copy. Turned points them at what is on the screen, and the readout says post-rotation so a number is never quietly about something other than its label. The level meter and the Clipping verdict stay on the signal either way: one is a modulation source and would feed back into the picture, and the other is a claim about the input.

Drawn cycle

Grab takes one cycle of what is playing, from the trigger lane: your input, or with the tone alone the generator's own output. Hold the same note on the keyboard and the period is the note's, exact; without one it is measured, and a few cents out is a cycle that does not quite close. The reading beside it says which, and its tooltip says the rest.

Nine sine partials at the footages of a tonewheel organ, drawn out from nought to eight. 8′ is the note you play; 16′ is an octave under it and 5⅓′ a fifth above that, so a registration with either out has a cycle twice the note's. Each step is about three decibels, as on the organ. However many bars are out the wave stays inside the amplitude: one bar at eight is a full-scale sine, and pulling out more changes the colour rather than the level. A partial above half the sample rate is left out rather than folded back. Every bar is a destination, so a drawbar on your keyboard, once it has moved, can be put on the same bar here. With a layer B, each layer has its own registration.

A second oscillator inside the voice, at Ratio times the note — the same kind of number as the interval between X and Y, and it is not a coincidence: a 3:2 modulator gives a harmonic sound exactly when a 3:2 figure closes. FM is how far it swings the voice's phase, from pure at nought to bright and then clangorous; above about ten on a sharp shape the top folds back. Warp bends the wave at one point of its cycle, Warp at, in degrees of it: turned up it pinches the wave there and swells it opposite, turned down the other way round, so the figure bulges or sharpens where you put it and the sound brightens either way. It is FM at one to one, locked to the note, so it stays in tune and stays harmonic, and a sharp shape bent the whole way at a high note folds back more than 40 dB down. A bent sine sits a little off the middle, because a pinched peak and a swollen trough no longer balance. Ring multiplies the voice by it instead, which removes the note and leaves the sum and the difference. Sync runs the shape faster than the note and restarts it at every note cycle, so the pitch stays and the tone tears; it is for the saw and the square. Sub mixes in a square or a sine an octave or two down. Unison stacks detuned copies, and the figure thickens and shimmers in place: the copies are not spread across left and right, because in X–Y that would smear one axis into the other. Behind the ⋯, the spread and the sub's octave and shape.

With a split or a layer, this is the layer being edited, like the shape. While sync is on, the voice is one sample late.

Shaping
off
off

Distortion inside the voice, before its envelope, so a note keeps its character as it fades. Drive pushes the wave into a soft ceiling: a sine rounds towards a square, and the reading is how much the quiet parts are lifted. Fold bends the wave back on itself each time it would pass full scale — on Y–T the peaks fold into the wave, in X–Y the figure grows petals, and it can take a source, so an LFO opens and closes them. Both are worked at twice the rate, so what they add above half the rate is filtered off; behind the ⋯, four times is cleaner for a hard drive on a high note, and costs twice as much for every voice, so it is for a few voices rather than a chord on two layers, and a chord too big for it is worked at twice anyway, which the readout says. Either way a shaped voice is 0.7 ms later. Crush and Rate are the opposite on purpose: fewer levels and fewer samples, the steps and the folding-back that a bitcrusher is bought for. Each layer has its own.

A filter in every note, after its shaping and before its level, so a low note and a high note can be equally bright and each note opens as it starts. It is the instrument's filter; the one called Filter is for looking, on the whole trace. Key track is how far the cutoff follows the note, all the way at a hundred, from middle C. Envelope is how many octaves its own envelope moves the cutoff, up or down; behind the ⋯ are that envelope's four, which work like the amplifier's and follow the keys the same way. The cutoff can take a source. On the dyad the two channels are filtered alike, each following its own pitch.

Oversampling

Things done to the picture of a stereo pair, the generator's or your input's, that turn out to be things done to its sound. Mirror folds the figure onto one half of itself, and to the ear it is full-wave rectification, the octave-up pedal: every harmonic even, the note an octave higher. The folded wave sits above zero, and the speakers get that offset unless AC coupling, under Vertical, takes it off. Radial clip holds the figure inside a circle of the radius and keeps every point's direction, so it is a clipper that does not bend the stereo image: loud parts are rounded off towards the circle, and quiet ones are nearly untouched. Both work on the picture and on what you hear, and in poly on the nearly-mono chord that you hear as well as on the pair that is drawn. With two layers, Layers gives B a plane and a Turn of its own, or keeps one for both.

Twist turns each point by an angle in proportion to how far it is from the middle: the loud parts swirl and the quiet middle stays still, a stereo rotation that depends on level. Fold at the radius reflects the figure back in each time it reaches the circle, a stereo-linked wavefolder. Snap puts both channels on a grid, a bitcrusher on the ear and pixels on the screen, at six bits or five. Behind this section's ⋯, Scale X and Scale Y are balance and width, and Shear feeds some of Y into X; those three are exact, and add no delay.

They run at twice the rate by default so that what they add above half the sample rate is filtered off rather than folded back as notes that are not in the key. Four times is cleaner still and costs twice as much; once is the arithmetic on its own. While any of the bending ones is on the pair is about 0.7 ms later, and switching one on moves the picture by that much.

After the plane, on the generator's figure and on what you hear. Echo is how loud the repeats are, and nought is off. In X–Y they are ghost figures trailing the live one; with Ping-pong each repeat comes back on the other channel, so the ghosts alternate between the figure and its reflection across the diagonal. Sync sets the time in note values from the tempo, on the Perform tab, and follows it. Feedback stops short of one, and nothing can be patched onto it: feedback that a source could push towards one would be a loop inside the loop. The longest time is two seconds.

Chorus is a copy of the pair a few milliseconds late, the lateness swinging at Rate, one channel's with a sine and the other's with its cosine, so the figure breathes and turns. Behind the ⋯, Depth is how far it swings, Centre how late it sits, and Feedback makes it a flanger: short, and fed back, it rings.

Phaser turns each harmonic by a different amount, sweeping at Sweep, one channel against the other, so in X–Y a line opens into a loop and a figure twists unevenly. Behind the ⋯, Range is how far it sweeps and Resonance sharpens its two notches. The picture's Memory brings it in on a picture that has stopped moving.

Reads

The screen read back as the voice's wave: sixty times a second the light is read round a circle near the figure, and that becomes one cycle of the sound, at the note you play. Depth is how much of the voice it is; at the top a fifth of the shape stays, so the note keeps its pitch. It is worth having where the picture moves: a still picture is a still wave, which is an ordinary tone. Softness blurs the light before it is read: at nought the thin lines read as spikes and buzz. Persistence is the menu over the screen in seconds: how long a stroke takes to fade to half, which is how much of what you played the wave remembers. Strike: every note lays light where Scan reads, as bright as you play it; at nought, none. With a split, Depth is the layer being edited, and Reads says whose picture each layer's Scan reads.

Score

A playhead crosses the screen at the tempo and plays what it passes: low on the screen is low in pitch, in the page's key, and the brightest points are the notes, the brightness how hard. Heard in the generator's voice; sent out too, if MIDI out has a port.

Screen reads
Speakers get

This shapes the trace, not the sound: a low pass rounds a square's corners toward a sine, a notch carves one harmonic out of the picture, and a resonant sweep draws its own ringing. It runs on the samples rather than in the audio graph, so it reaches the test tone as well — which is arithmetic and has no audio graph at all. Resonance is nought for gentle and a hundred for extreme; at nought a low pass is maximally flat. Resonance boosts at the corner, so a high setting can push the trace past full scale and the readout will say Clipping — which is true, and is why nothing quietly turns it down: a compressor on the screen would make the trace lie about the level. Drop Full scale under Vertical, or the amplitude.

The two switches are separate because they answer different questions, and they straddle the same block: the filter, the AC coupling and the X–Y rotation, in that order. Screen shaped, speakers input is the block as an instrument for looking. Both shaped is the ordinary sense. Screen input, speakers shaped lets you watch what you are feeding it, and the readout says screen on the input so a flat trace under a filtered sound is never a mystery — and speakers on the input the other way round, because a sweep on the graticule over a plain tone is the same confusion mirrored. Neither is said when there is nothing switched on for them to differ about. Anything that reaches the speakers passes a limiter first, which is not a taste decision: resonance is something a source can sweep, and a resonant peak swept upward is a loud surprise in a pair of headphones.

The screen’s switch used to straddle the filter alone while the speakers’ straddled all three, so Input meant one thing to the eyes and another to the ears — on a page whose argument is that they are the same block. The lag is the one thing still outside it, because the speakers have no lag to bypass yet.

Shaped is the filter and the X–Y rotation, and the rotation is the interesting one: turning a figure and rotating a stereo image are the same 2×2 matrix, so the control that exists to make the picture prettier is a real stereo operation and this is where you hear it. Both are driven from one set of numbers — the screen and the speakers cannot disagree about what a rotation is, and a test renders the graph and checks it against the arithmetic.

Rotation is seen whether or not it is heard, and on a stereo pair it reaches the Y–T lanes and the trigger as well as the figure — it is a transform on the signal, so it is in the block before anything looks at it. What it does not reach is the numbers: those read Signal by default, under Display, and stay about what arrived. The level meter and the Clipping verdict stay there whatever that switch says. Turning the stereo image can put up to 41% more into one channel than either started with, which the limiter and the clamp are still the last things before.

Position is how much of the window sits before the edge — the run-up to the event rather than only what followed it. Holdoff rejects an edge that has another one close behind it, which is what settles a waveform crossing the level more than once a cycle.

Beam

On a real scope the spot's brightness is how long it dwelt, so it goes as one over its speed — bright where the trace turns around, faint through the fast sweeps. Off for the waveform by default: dimming the steep edge of a square wave fights the job Y–T is for.

Oscilloscope
